entry.title: Matins Readings
entry.content:
In the latest issue of Ephemerides Liturgicae, my extensive study on the biblical, patristic, and hagiographic pericopes contained in the 1957 edition of the “Breviarium Ambrosianum” was published.

On the biblical side, one notes the substantial preservation of the ordo set out by Beroldus in the 12th century; the selection of patristic texts is marked by a prevalence of Ambrosian and Augustinian writings, though other authors are not absent; the lives of the saints, on the other hand, have undergone continual processes of updating in periods following the Council of Trent. The composite form of this document is a valuable historical witness to a multifaceted stratification, whose study may open the way to further investigations.
entry.summary: A study on the matins readings in the last edition of the Ambrosian Breviary

entry.title: NLP for Digital Humanities
entry.content:
Today my recent research was published in the scientific journal Umanistica Digitale.

This article offers a survey of recent studies on the application of Natural Language Processing techniques to classical philology, with particular emphasis on Latin epic poetry of the 1st century AD. Although originally designed for the analysis of modern languages, the algorithms developed in computational linguistics over the past three decades – ranging from Latent Semantic Allocation and Latent Dirichlet Allocation to the more recent Transformer models based on Neural Networks – have transformed intertextual research through the practice of Topic Extraction. Particular attention is given to cases aimed at detecting situational correspondences even in the absence of co-occurring vocabulary. The examples discussed confirm both the efficacy of this approach and the convergence between ‘traditional’ philological methods and computational-linguistic techniques.
entry.summary: Applications of Digital Analysis Techniques to Classical Languages and Literatures
